title: Fine Bikes: Framebuilding as a Love Language – Spencer Harding
content:
In the wake of this year’s Made, Spencer made a special post-show trip to shoot two very special bikes from Raleigh, NC-based Fine Bikes. Charles and Adeline of Fine Bikes were to be married a few days after the show and then whisked off on a honeymoon tour on these two bespoke bikes. Check out the love-filled gallery below…

At the 2025 Made show, one of the first bikes I shot was Adeline’s new road bike that Charles had built for her. It was covered in hearts, and as with many framebuilding endeavours, full of love. There was something special hidden in the bike that neither me nor Adeline knew about at the time: an engagement ring. Hidden in the frame throughout the show and retrieved on a ride a few days after the show, Charles proposed. I got wind of this love story after the show, and it quickly became a favorite story to relate when people asked: “How was bike show?” There are so many eye-wateringly impressive bikes at the show, but a road bike from Raleigh and its owner and crafter stole the show in my eyes.

When I caught up with Charles and Adeline at this year’s Made, as they assembled their new steeds, they mentioned they were gonna get married a few days after the show. I was flabbergasted, then Charles pointed to another bag, which he said had their wedding outfits. Right then, an idea came to me: this needed to be something more special than a grimey shoot on the side of an abandoned shipyard. It didn’t wind up being much more romantic in the neighborhood of their Airbnb as the last light hit on Sunday, but the light was surely more romantic. Two guys sitting on the porch drinking beers were our witnesses; they’d actually been at the show that weekend, as Charles and Adeline posed with their bikes in their wedding finest. I’ve nearly always deigned to be an engagement or wedding photographer, but this moment felt like it deserved ditching of long-held notions; for love and bikes.

Adeline’s Fine Bike

Charles described this bike as a modern gravel/ commuter rig by the numbers, but the aesthetics are a proper melding of modern and classic. The paint and detailing were inspired by a tanker truck from their last big bike tour in 2023, and oh, does that glitter shine. Don’t miss the details on the seat tube and fork blades.

The frame is primarily Reynolds 853 with a segmented fork topped so elegantly with custom racks also fabricated by Charles. The rack was chrome-plated locally by East Tennessee Plating. In the failing light of the day, the rack truly sang, and as it has become a theme, look at that heart on the top deck of the rack.

Classiqué styling of the Velo Orange saddle, silver fenders, and square taper cranks and bottom bracket blend seamlessly with more modern disc brakes, 1x wide range drivetrain, and a threadless steerer. From the Madrone derailleur to the Klampers to the 100% cranks to the brake levers to the seatpost and finally the headset, her bike is shiiiiiiiiiny. Thank goodness I got to shoot it in the shade or I might have been blinded.

Charles’ Fine Bike

Charles’ take on a classic French randonneur bike from the 1950s, pulling inspiration from hours of oogling Brain Chapman, JP Weigle and Mitch Pryor. The impetus for this particular build started around a very specific set of brakes, the Mafac Raid calipers. He first became aware of this style of brake when Paul released their Racer brakes styled after the Mafac Racers, which started Charles down a long rabbit hole that eventually led to this very bike.

The lugs are old stamped specimens he acquired from a retired builder in Raleigh that he heavily modified to his liking. Charles tried to use as much old tubing as he could scrounge from older builders and his own stock, making the bike all the more impressive since it won accolades at the show. I really love the details such as the spoke holder- real touring nerds will know- and the cable hangers. The build is bejeweled in Randonneur classic parts, but those Mafac Raid brakes really steal the show, almost as if the bike was built around them.

The paint scheme was inspired by a chance moto helmet sighting at a coffee shop. A friend gifted Charles a Buegler for the pinstriping the fenders, and he hand-painted the lugs with a liquid writer. Don’t miss the custom art on the rear fender from GHOOOST!

As with Adeline’s bike, he custom fabricated the stem and racks, which were sent off for chrome plating. The Silca pump, one he’d had forever, was stripped and paint-matched as well. To top off an incredibly shiny build, he even treated himself to a shiny new SON dynamo hub.

The amount of love that goes into a pile of steel tubes, lugs, and parts Charles had lying around, only to manifest in such a stunning bike, is staggering and a monument to his talent and care.

As I wrap up my thoughts about the Made show, I can sometimes scarcely remember what bikes I saw, or what cool new gadget I encountered, but I can remember all the people I hugged. Maybe I hadn’t even seen some of those people since the last Made show, but that is just fine; life happens. I was lucky enough to spend a weekend with Charles and Adeline at Bike Camp in Chattanooga this past spring in the interim, and it’s been truly lovely to get to know them a bit better and have a view into this time when they are solidifying their love for each other. Last year these two won my heart with their engagement bike, and this year they have returned to further that love with two more bikes heading straight to their honeymoon bike tour. Charles and Adeline win hearts again.
